verses.translation_literal: And it was, when Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim from seeing, that he called Esau his son, the elder, and said to him, "My son." And he said to him, "Here I am."
verses.translation_dramatic: Isaac had grown old, and the world had begun to dim before his eyes, until faces were shadows and shapes had no edges. In that dusk he sent for Esau, his elder son, and spoke the one word a father says when he is about to ask for everything: "My son." And out of the room's quiet came the ready answer: "Here I am."
verses.directors_commentary: Isaac is old and nearly blind, and that failing sight is the hinge of the whole chapter: a scene about seeing and being seen, in which everyone else will act in the dark of his eyes. The KJV's "so that he could not see" turns the Hebrew's mere "from seeing" into a result clause; the Hebrew says the eyes were too dim for sight, not that he saw nothing. Notice that the narrator says "Esau his son, the elder" before Jacob has appeared: the order of birth is stated up front, since the whole drama is about who receives what that order promises. The exchange "My son" / "Here I am" (hineni) is the formal call-and-answer of Genesis, the same word Abraham gave Isaac on Moriah; play it as readiness, not as ordinary politeness. Rashi offers the tradition that the dimness began at the binding when angels' tears fell on Isaac's eyes, while Rashbam, Radak and Sforno read it as ordinary age (Rashbam compares Eli).

philological_notes.note: 'To grow dim, faint.' The verb is plural feminine, agreeing with 'eyes' (a grammatically feminine noun). The same verb is used of Eli's failing sight in 1 Samuel 3:13 and 4:15 and of Jacob's in Gen 48:10 (using a different verb, kaved). Here it states a condition, not yet a cause.

'Here I am': the formal answer of one who stands attentive and available. It is exactly Abraham's answer to God and to Isaac in Genesis 22; Esau uses the same word to his father here, and Isaac will later ask 'Who are you, my son?' of the one who answers.

verses.translation_literal: And he said, "Behold now, I have grown old; I have not known the day of my death."
verses.translation_dramatic: "Look at me," he said. "I am old now. I do not know the day of my death."
verses.directors_commentary: Isaac does not say he is dying; he says he cannot know when. That is the precise fear of a man who has a duty left undone: a blessing must be spoken while the speaker has breath and lucidity, and death may come without warning. Radak reads it just so: he may die suddenly and be unable to bless. Rashi counts the years instead: Isaac, at 123, reckons that he may be near the age at which his mother died, which is why the day is uncertain. The KJV is accurate here ("I know not the day"), but its "Behold now" hides the plain urgency of the Hebrew particles hineh-na, "look, please": an old man asking to be listened to. Play the speech quietly, as someone arranging his affairs and not as an invalid.

philological_notes.note: A softened call for attention, 'look now, please'. Ibn Ezra glosses it 'now'. It marks Isaac's request as polite and urgent together.

'I have not known the day of my death': the perfect tense states a present condition, 'I do not know'. Radak reads it as fear of a sudden death that would cut the blessing short; Sforno adds that a blessing takes hold more strongly when the blesser is near death.

verses.translation_literal: "And now, take up, please, your gear, your quiver and your bow, and go out to the field and hunt for me game."
verses.translation_dramatic: "So now," said Isaac, "take up your gear: the quiver, the bow. Go out to the open country and hunt for me. Bring me game."
verses.directors_commentary: This is the order that sets Esau in motion, and Isaac gives it with courtesy ("please") and with a list of tools, as if naming the kit were itself part of the pleasure of the request. "Take up" (sa') is the verb of lifting a load, which the KJV drops with "take". The KJV also gives "venison", which in 1611 meant any hunted meat; to modern ears it means deer and quietly narrows the Hebrew tzayid, "game", which can be any wild animal or bird. "The field" (hasadeh) is open country, the opposite of the tent: Esau is introduced in Genesis 25 as a man of the field, and Jacob as one who dwells in tents. The word "quiver" (teli) occurs only here, and its meaning is uncertain: Rashi and Onkelos say "sword", Radak says quiver, and the pairing with bow favors quiver. Radak notes that Esau did not go out every day, so this was an errand with a purpose.

philological_notes.note: A word found only here, from 'to hang' (the thing hung on the shoulder or belt). Rashbam and Radak take it as the quiver; Rashi, as the sword that is hung. The versions follow the quiver.

'Game, hunted food'. The Masoretic note records that the word is written with a final he (tzayidah) but read without it. Radak mentions a midrash seeing a hint to five laws of slaughter in the extra letter. The verb 'hunt' (tzudah) and the noun 'game' (tzayid) share a root, a repetition I keep in the literal layer.

token_glosses.gloss: game (written: with final he; read: tzayid)

verses.translation_literal: "And make for me savory dishes, as I love, and bring [them] to me, and I will eat, in order that my soul may bless you before I die."
verses.translation_dramatic: "Then cook it for me the way I love it: the rich, savory dishes that wake an old man's tongue. Bring them to me and let me eat, so that my soul may bless you before I die."
verses.directors_commentary: Isaac asks for a meal and a blessing in one sentence, and the link between them ("in order that", ba'avur) is the hinge on which the story turns. The word mat'ammim means dishes made to the taste, from ta'am, "taste": it is not the KJV's "savoury meat", where "meat" meant food in 1611 and now misleads. Radak says it is not need that drives the request, since Isaac is rich, but an old man's longing for something new and well-flavored. The phrase "my soul may bless you" (nafshi) places the blessing in the whole self, not only in the mouth: this is a rite in which the appetite and the blessing are bound together, and the sources of the meal become part of the transaction. Ramban reads the intention as to give the firstborn the blessing of Abraham; Sforno, that the act of service to a father makes the blessing take hold. Notice the verb sequence: bring, eat, bless. Esau is asked for a service; he is not told what it is for.

philological_notes.note: 'Tasty things, dishes made to taste'. From ta'am, 'taste, flavor', the same root as in the verb 'to taste'. The word occurs only in this chapter (vv. 4, 7, 9, 14, 17, 31).

Nefesh is the self, the appetite and the life together. 'My soul may bless you' means the whole person blesses, and the blessing is to be spoken from satisfaction. When Rebekah repeats the plan in v. 7 she says 'I will bless you', and in v. 10 'he may bless you', and 'my soul' does not recur.

verses.translation_literal: And Rebekah was listening when Isaac spoke to Esau his son. And Esau went to the field to hunt game to bring [it].
verses.translation_dramatic: But Rebekah was listening. She stood within earshot while Isaac spoke to Esau, his son, and she heard every word. Then Esau went out to the field, to hunt for game and bring it home.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse turns on a participle: Rebekah is shomaat, "listening", a continuing action in the background of the scene, while the men speak. The KJV's "heard" is a simple past that tells us she overheard; the Hebrew makes her an active, standing presence, and the narrator does not say she was invited. The contrast is tight: Isaac speaks to "Esau his son", and Rebekah is listening, with no "her son" yet to come. Rashi's gloss on "to bring" asks what the phrase adds: if he cannot find game he will bring it from somewhere else, even by theft; I treat that as his midrash, not the plain sense. Radak reads Rebekah's response as jealousy at seeing Esau go to fulfill his father's wish. Nothing in the verse tells us what she thinks; give the actress the pause and do not fill it.

philological_notes.note: A feminine participle: 'was listening, was hearing'. It marks continuing action and frames the scene from behind Isaac and Esau. In Hebrew shama' means both to hear and to heed, a double sense that matters for v. 8.

verses.translation_literal: And Rebekah said to Jacob her son, saying, "Behold, I have heard your father speaking to Esau your brother, saying,"
verses.translation_dramatic: Rebekah went to Jacob, her son. "Listen," she said. "I have just heard your father speaking to Esau, your brother. This is what he said:"
verses.directors_commentary: The text now names the sides. Isaac had "Esau his son"; Rebekah has "Jacob her son". And inside her report the roles shift again: Isaac is "your father" and Esau is "your brother", so that the conversation she repeats is framed as something Jacob has a stake in. The KJV's "I heard thy father speak" is correct but hides the participle "speaking": she heard it as it was happening. The phrase "saying ... saying" (le'mor) opens a quotation inside a quotation: she is about to report Isaac's words, and her report will not be exact. Compare the next verse with Isaac's own words in v. 4 and watch what she adds. Radak says the whole speech is her way to bring her son into the scheme.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'to say', a quotation marker that opens direct speech. Here it appears twice, so that Rebekah's own words contain Isaac's. The second le'mor introduces her report.

verses.translation_literal: "Bring me game and make me savory dishes, and I will eat, and I will bless you before YHWH before my death."
verses.translation_dramatic: "Bring me game," he said, "and make me the dishes I love, and I will eat. And then I will bless you, in the presence of the LORD, before I die."
verses.directors_commentary: Compare this with Isaac's actual words in verse 4. He said: bring, eat, "my soul may bless you before I die." Rebekah says: "I will bless you before YHWH before my death." The phrase "before YHWH" is hers; Isaac never said it. It lifts an old man's request for a meal and a blessing into a solemn act done in the presence of God, and Ramban observes that the phrase is not found anywhere else in the whole passage of the blessing. Radak says she added it to make Jacob feel the weight of the thing; Ramban takes it as her way of telling him that the blessing, once given, will stand before God and cannot be reversed. Rashi glosses "before YHWH" as "with His consent". The KJV renders it correctly, but it cannot show that Rebekah, not Isaac, put the divine name into the scene. Rashbam compares Nimrod, "a mighty hunter before the LORD", where the phrase means in the world, not literally in His sight. Play the shift: she is no longer reporting, she is persuading.

philological_notes.note: 'Before YHWH': in His presence, with His sanction. Absent from Isaac's own words in v. 4. Rashi reads it as 'with His consent'; Rashbam notes that elsewhere (Gen 10:9) it can be an intensifier; Radak and Ramban read it as Rebekah's emphasis.

verses.translation_literal: "And now, my son, listen to my voice, to what I am commanding you."
verses.translation_dramatic: "So now, my son, listen to me. Do what I tell you."
verses.directors_commentary: The word "now" (ve'attah) turns the report into an order. Rebekah, who a moment ago was quoting Isaac, now gives a command of her own, and she uses the verb for it, mtzavvah, "I am commanding": this is the language of a parent's authority. The KJV's "obey my voice" is closer than most, since the Hebrew idiom shema' beqol means both listen to and obey. The pronoun "I" (ani) is stated although the verb already contains it, and that emphasis sets her voice against Isaac's. The theme of the "voice" will return in verse 22, when Isaac says that the voice is Jacob's voice. Radak ties the next instruction, to go to the flock, to the same sentence. Here it should land as a command from a woman who has already decided.

philological_notes.note: 'Listen to my voice' means 'obey me'. The sound of the word voice (qol) is the thread of the chapter: Isaac will know a voice before he knows a hand.
'Commanding', a participle: the command is issued now and continues. It is the verb of authority; the explicit 'I' before it stresses whose command this is.

verses.translation_literal: "Go, please, to the flock and take for me from there two kids of the goats, good ones, and I will make them savory dishes for your father, as he loves."
verses.translation_dramatic: "Go to the flock," she said. "Choose two kids from the goats, two fine ones, and bring them to me. I will turn them into the savory dishes your father loves."
verses.directors_commentary: Here the plan becomes concrete, and it is a plan about food: two young goats from the household's own flock, cooked as Isaac likes them. The KJV's "thence" and "savoury meat" are archaic but not wrong; what it cannot show is that Isaac's "as I love" in v. 4 has become "as he loves", Rebekah's claim to know her husband's palate. The taste of kid, Rashi says, is like that of game, which is why the substitution can work. Rashi also records the midrash that the kids are Rebekah's by right, so that the act involves no theft; and Rashbam observes that Jacob, the tent-dweller, is sent to the flock, his own trade. Radak glosses "good" (tovim) as fat, and the point is real: this is a meal chosen for richness. The asking of "please" (na') softens the order of v. 8. Rebekah is mother and strategist at once: a command, but a polite one.

philological_notes.note: 'Kids of the goats': young goats. Rashbam says goats are chosen because their skins carry hair as coarse as a man's, which prepares for the disguise in vv. 15-16; Rashi, relying on Pirkei de-Rabbi Eliezer, asks why two kids for one meal, and answers that one served as the Passover offering.
'Good', here in the sense of choice or fat, as Radak says, citing the 'tender and good' calf of Gen 18:7.

verses.translation_literal: "And you will bring [it] to your father, and he will eat, in order that he may bless you before his death."
verses.translation_dramatic: "You will carry it in to your father, and he will eat. And then he will bless you, before he dies."
verses.directors_commentary: Rebekah ends the plan by closing the circle: bring, eat, bless. Set it beside verse 4: Isaac said "my soul may bless you", and Rebekah drops "my soul" and says simply "he may bless you", with the one change that matters, "you", Jacob, where Isaac meant Esau. The verbs are Isaac's, the goal is hers. Also notice the three futures in a row ("you will bring", "he will eat", "he may bless"), which make it sound like a settled schedule, not a risk. The KJV's "thou shalt bring" reads as a command; the Hebrew form is a plain future, and that confidence is part of her persuasion. Nothing in the verse mentions the disguise yet, and the actors should not play it as if it did.

philological_notes.note: 'In order that': the same purpose phrase as ba'avur in v. 4, here with asher and a spelling without the vav. It repeats Isaac's own link between the meal and the blessing.

verses.translation_literal: And Jacob said to Rebekah his mother, "Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man."
verses.translation_dramatic: Jacob answered his mother. He did not say no, and he did not say yes. "Look," he said, "Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a man with smooth skin."
verses.directors_commentary: Jacob's first words in the scene are not about right or wrong but about skin. The Hebrew is a pair of mirror clauses, "a man hairy" and "a man smooth", with the same word ish (man) in each, so that the brothers are set side by side as two kinds of body. The KJV's "hairy man" and "smooth man" are right; the Hebrew shaar (hairy) echoes Seir, the land that Esau will inherit, and Esau's own red and hairy birth in Genesis 25. The word "behold" (hen) is Jacob's objection raised as a plain fact. Radak says Esau was covered with hair even on his hands and neck. Notice also that Jacob speaks to "Rebekah his mother", the mirror of her "Jacob her son" in v. 6: the family is being drawn in pairs. Do not play it as a refusal; play it as a man looking for the flaw in the plan.

philological_notes.note: 'Hairy'. The same consonants form the name Seir, the highland of Edom, and the word for 'goat' (se'ir, from the same root). The sound-play quietly joins Esau, Edom and the goat skins that will cover Jacob's arms (my own reading). Rashi glosses the phrase 'ish sa'ir' as 'a possessor of hair'; Radak says the hair covered even his hands and neck.
'Smooth': of skin without hair. Ibn Ezra relates it to the sense of 'even, uniform'.

verses.translation_literal: "Perhaps my father will feel me, and I will be in his eyes like a mocker, and I will bring upon myself a curse and not a blessing."
verses.translation_dramatic: "Perhaps my father will touch me. Then I will stand before him as a mocker, a man making sport of a blind old man's trust, and I will bring down on my own head a curse instead of a blessing."
verses.directors_commentary: Jacob's objection is not that the deed is wrong; it is that he might be caught. His fear is concrete: his father will run a hand over him, and he will be found out. The KJV renders the key word as "deceiver"; the Hebrew mit'atea' is stronger, one who mocks or makes sport, from a root that suggests toying with someone, and Radak explains it as "how you made a fool of me!". Note the phrase "in his eyes": the blind man's "eyes" return, so that Jacob will be judged by the sight of a man who cannot see. Jacob measures the cost with a stark pair, "a curse and not a blessing", and the same noun brakhah that Isaac had set at the center of the chapter. "I will bring upon myself" shows he sees the consequence as self-inflicted. Ramban wonders why Jacob fears the touch and not the voice, and offers two ideas; the text itself leaves the question open, and the later scene will answer it.

philological_notes.note: 'He will feel me': to grope, to touch by hand, the verb of the blind groping at noon (Deut 28:29, the parallel Rashi draws). The sense is of a blind man's hand feeling his way, which fits Isaac perfectly.

'Like a mocker, a trifler': from a root of mocking and misleading, found in 'mockery' (Jer 10:15) and in 2 Chronicles 36:16. Radak glosses it as playing a trick on someone who cannot see. The word is rare and stronger than 'deceiver'.

'A curse': from a root meaning 'to make light of, to treat as of no weight', the opposite of blessing, which is from a root of weight and abundance. The pair 'curse and not a blessing' is the chapter's central contrast.

verses.translation_literal: And she said to him, his mother, "On me [be] your curse, my son. Only listen to my voice, and go, take [them] for me."
verses.translation_dramatic: His mother did not hesitate. "Let the curse fall on me, my son," she said, and her voice was low and certain. "On me, not on you. Only do as I say: listen to my voice, go, and bring them to me."
verses.directors_commentary: Rebekah does not argue the moral question; she moves the risk onto herself. 'On me be your curse' is the language of someone taking on liability, like a surety in a household where a spoken curse was believed to travel and land. The KJV's 'Upon me be thy curse' is close and rightly keeps the stark word 'curse' (qelalah); BBE's 'Let the curse be on me' adds a wish the Hebrew does not voice, because the Hebrew has no verb, just the clipped nominal clause. Then three short imperatives in a row: listen, go, take. A mother who has made up her mind speaks in commands. Note the twin 'listen to my voice' (shema' bekoli): this is the verse where voice becomes the chapter's key, since it will be Jacob's voice that gives him away in v. 22. KJV's 'obey' is acceptable, but the Hebrew is simply 'hear', and the pun on hearing the voice runs on.

philological_notes.note: A verbless clause: 'on me your curse'. Rebekah takes the penalty of a curse onto herself. The commentators split on whether this rests on a prophecy she received (Onkelos; Rashbam, pointing to 'the elder shall serve the younger') or is a mother's confidence (Ibn Ezra, Radak). The text itself gives no reason.
'Listen to my voice' is the ordinary Hebrew idiom for obeying. It also plants the word 'voice' (qol), which will decide the scene in v. 22.

verses.translation_literal: And he went, and he took, and he brought [them] to his mother; and his mother made savory foods, as his father loved.
verses.translation_dramatic: So he went. He took the kids, he carried them in to his mother, and she set to work. By the time she was done the tent smelled of everything his father loved: savory, rich and seasoned just so.
verses.directors_commentary: Three verbs in a row, 'went, took, brought', and Jacob has no lines at all. After his objection in v. 12 he simply does it; the text withholds his inner life, and the actor must decide where the reluctance goes. Rebekah, by contrast, is the grammatical subject of the cooking, which sets the pattern: she is the doer, he the hands. 'Matamim' is a seasoned, flavoured dish (from ta'am, 'taste'), and the KJV's 'savoury meat' is fine in its time but misleads today: 'meat' then meant any food, and here it is specifically goat, spiced to Isaac's taste (Radak on 27:17). The clause 'as his father loved' echoes 25:28, where Isaac loved Esau because of the game in his mouth; Rebekah knows how to reach Isaac through his appetite.

philological_notes.note: 'Tasty dishes', from the root for taste. Not 'meat' but seasoned food; Radak says the meat is the core of it and that it was dressed with fine spices.

verses.translation_literal: And Rebekah took the clothes of Esau, her son, the elder, the desirable ones, which [were] with her in the house, and she clothed Jacob, her son, the younger.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then Rebekah went to the chest in the house and drew out Esau's clothes, the elder son's best, the garments men envy. She dressed Jacob in them, her younger son, as one dresses a child for a feast.
verses.directors_commentary: The verse is built on two parallel phrases: 'Esau her son, the elder' and 'Jacob her son, the younger'. The text does not say 'her favourite'; it only lays the two side by side, and Ramban hears in it the pointed arithmetic of birth order that she is about to overturn. 'The desirable ones' (hachamudot) are Esau's finest clothes, kept in her keeping: the KJV's 'goodly raiment' loses the verb of desire in the word, since these are garments that others would covet. Radak says Esau wore them on formal occasions and that they were scented with field herbs; that is why Isaac will later smell 'the smell of a field' (v. 27). Whether that is the text's meaning or later reading, the idea that Esau's clothes are held by Rebekah, and not by his own wives, has drawn comment: Rashi sees in it Esau's distrust of his wives.

philological_notes.note: 'The desirable things', from the root of coveting (as in 'you shall not covet'). Rashi, following the Targum, reads it as 'the clean ones'; Rashbam says Esau served his father in them at meals; Radak that they were festive dress perfumed with field herbs.

verses.translation_literal: And [obj] the skins of the kids of the goats she clothed [on] his hands, and on the smooth part of his neck.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the skins of the young goats, still faintly warm and rank, she bound over his hands and over the bare smooth place at the back of his neck.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb is the same as in v. 15: she 'clothed' (hilbish) him in garments, then clothed his hands in skins. The Hebrew repeats it, so the English should too; the disguise is a wardrobe. 'Smooth part' (chelqat) names the hairless skin of the neck, the one patch of Jacob that would feel different from his brother's; the same root gives Jacob's own word 'smooth' in v. 11 (chalaq) when he objects that Esau is hairy and he is smooth. KJV 'the smooth of his neck' is literal but clumsy, and nobody hears the echo. Radak says the purpose was touch and smell. Whether the skins were treated to feel like hair (Sforno) is inference, not text. Note also that 'the kids of the goats' is the stock phrase: the same animals Rebekah has just cooked supply the disguise, so the meal and the costume come from one source.

philological_notes.note: 'The smooth part of his neck'. It picks up Jacob's own objection that he is a 'smooth' man (v. 11). The plural 'necks' is a plural of the part, as often.

verses.translation_literal: And she gave the savory foods and the bread which she had made into the hand of Jacob, her son.
verses.translation_dramatic: Last she put the dishes into his hands, the savory food and the bread she had baked, and closed his fingers around the weight of it. Her son, now ready to go in.
verses.directors_commentary: 'Into the hand of Jacob her son': the verse ends on his hand, the hand that has just been covered with goatskin. The camera should linger there. The 'bread' (lechem) is easily lost; Radak notes that she made it fresh and hot, so the meal feels real. KJV and ASV 'meat' for matamim is the old sense of 'food', a pitfall for today's reader.

verses.translation_literal: And he came to his father, and he said, "My father." And he said, "Here I [am]. Who [are] you, my son?"
verses.translation_dramatic: He came in to his father and said, softly, "My father." And out of the dim room came the answer: "Here I am." Then, quick behind it: "Who are you, my son?"
verses.directors_commentary: Jacob says only one word, 'father' (avi), and the old man's first question is already 'Who?'. Radak: once Isaac heard the voice, he doubted it. Everything that follows rests on a blind man's ears. Isaac's 'Hineni', 'here I am', is the ritual reply of a man standing ready (as Abraham answered at Moriah, 22:1); here it is the opening of a trap. KJV reproduces the Hebrew well; the point to bring out is that Jacob avoids the name altogether. He says 'my father' and receives 'my son'; the intimate words carry the lie before Jacob has to tell it.

philological_notes.note: 'Here I am': the stock reply of readiness, with the doubled nun carrying the suffix. Radak notes the doubled nun.

verses.translation_literal: And Jacob said to his father, "I, Esau, your firstborn. I have done as you spoke to me. Arise, please, sit, and eat of my game, in order that your soul may bless me."
verses.translation_dramatic: "I am Esau," said Jacob, "your firstborn." His voice held steady. "I have done what you told me. Sit up, Father, please, and eat of my hunting, so that your soul may bless me."
verses.directors_commentary: The great lie of the chapter, in six words, and the Hebrew has no 'am': 'I, Esau, your firstborn'. That bare clause is ambiguous, and Rashi, reading it as 'I am the one bringing it, and Esau is your firstborn', takes it as technically true; Radak and Ibn Ezra, by contrast, defend Jacob by pointing to prophecy and to his mother's command. Whatever one decides, the text puts the lie in Jacob's mouth and lets it stand. Then he does as Esau would: 'Arise, please, sit': a courteous, almost wheedling tone (Rashi on 27:22 hears 'supplication' in it). KJV 'venison' is a trap: it meant any hunted game, not deer in particular, and Hebrew tsayid is simply 'game, hunting'. 'Your soul' (nafshekha) for 'you' is the language of Isaac's own earlier request (v. 4) that his soul bless; Jacob is quoting his father's own wish back to him. 'Sit' (shevah) means to recline to eat, to sit at table (Rashi on 27:19).

philological_notes.note: A verbless clause: 'I, Esau, your firstborn'. It may be read as a direct claim to be Esau, or, with a pause after anokhi, as Rashi has it: 'I [am the one bringing it]; Esau is your firstborn'. The commentators defend or excuse Jacob on other grounds as well.
'Sit', here in the sense of reclining at the table to eat.
'Your soul', that is 'you', but with the weight of the whole self, the seat of appetite and blessing.

verses.translation_literal: And Isaac said to his son, "What [is] this, you have hurried to find, my son?" And he said, "Because YHWH your God made [it] meet before me."
verses.translation_dramatic: Isaac turned his face toward his son. "How is this? You found it so quickly, my son." And Jacob answered, without a pause, "Because the LORD your God put it in my path."
verses.directors_commentary: Isaac's unease shows: the voice is not quite right, and the hunt was too quick (Radak). Jacob's answer is the most dangerous line of the scene, since he drags God in: not 'my God' but 'YHWH your God', the phrase of a man speaking to a father of faith, or of someone keeping God at arm's length. Rashi hears it as a slip, since Esau would not have had the divine name so ready, and that is part of why Isaac asks to touch him next (Rashi on 27:21). The verb hiqrah is from the root 'to meet, happen' (the root of miqreh, 'chance'): God arranged the encounter. KJV 'brought it to me' flattens this; ASV 'sent me good speed' invents a phrase. Notice Jacob puts into God's hand the very thing he has taken from his brother.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of qarah, 'to meet, to happen': 'caused to meet', that is, God put the animal in his way. Related to miqreh, 'chance'.
'YHWH your God': Rashi reads the unusual piety as what makes Isaac suspicious, because it is not Esau's way to have the divine name on his lips.

verses.translation_literal: And Isaac said to Jacob, "Draw near, please, and let me feel you, my son: [are] you this, my son Esau, or not?"
verses.translation_dramatic: Isaac was silent a moment. Then: "Come closer, my son. Let me touch you." His hand lifted in the dark. "Are you truly my son Esau, or not?"
verses.directors_commentary: Blind Isaac asks, in effect, for the one test he has left. The question 'Esau or not?' (im lo) is blunt: he is giving Jacob one more chance to confess. Rashi: Isaac thinks that Esau would never have God's name so quickly on his lips, hence the test. Ramban doubts that Esau was wicked in his father's eyes and suggests the doubt rests on the voice. 'Feel' (mashash) is a groping touch, the verb used for a blind man in the dark (Deut 28:29). KJV's 'my very son Esau' adds 'very' for emphasis that the Hebrew does not have; the Hebrew simply points: 'this one, my son Esau'.

philological_notes.note: 'And I will feel you': a verb of groping by touch, first used in v. 12 when Jacob feared this very thing ('perhaps my father will feel me'). Radak and Ibn Ezra comment on the unusual vocalization, without the expected doubling of the shin.

verses.translation_literal: And Jacob drew near to Isaac his father, and he felt him, and he said, "The voice, [the] voice of Jacob, and the hands, [the] hands of Esau."
verses.translation_dramatic: Jacob stepped forward. The old hands found him, moved over the skins on his wrists, and stopped. "The voice," Isaac said slowly, "is the voice of Jacob. But the hands... the hands are the hands of Esau."
verses.directors_commentary: The whole chapter turns on two ears and ten fingers. The Hebrew is balanced like a scale: 'the voice, the voice of Jacob; and the hands, the hands of Esau'. Each noun is repeated, which English can keep by repeating it. The KJV's 'the voice is Jacob's voice' keeps the repetition; BBE loses it. Commentators split on why the voice misled him: Rashbam says the twins' voices were alike; Rashi that Jacob's polite speech ('arise, please') betrays him, as Esau would have said something curt. Radak notes that Isaac only touched the hands, not the neck. Sforno wonders whether his touch had failed with age. Take the line as Isaac's honest confusion, and play the moment of silence after it.

philological_notes.note: 'And he felt him': the same root as in v. 12 and v. 21; Jacob's fear is now realized.

A chiastic pair of nominal clauses ('the voice, the voice of Jacob; the hands, the hands of Esau'). Rashi hears in Jacob's voice the language of entreaty; Rashbam, a likeness between the twins' voices.

verses.translation_literal: And he did not recognize him, because his hands were like the hands of Esau his brother, hairy; and he blessed him.
verses.translation_dramatic: He did not know him. The hands under his fingers were rough and thick with hair, his brother's hands, and so Isaac gave him what he had asked for. He blessed him.
verses.directors_commentary: The narrator's verdict arrives in one breath: 'he did not recognize him' (lo hikiro), and the verb is the same used for the failure to recognize at the heart of Joseph's story later. The word 'hairy' (se'irot) shares its consonants with Seir, Esau's later land, and with se'ir, 'goat'; whether the text intends the play is my own reading, but the goatskin is certainly more than a costume. KJV 'discerned' is a Latinate word for 'recognized'; BBE 'make out' is better. The last word, 'and he blessed him', arrives before the full blessing itself (v. 27 ff.), so many take it as the beginning of the act, and Sforno links it to Isaac's suspicion: having suspected his son unjustly, Isaac is owed no apology but a blessing, as with Eli and Hannah.

philological_notes.note: 'He recognized him'. The same root gives 'stranger' (nokhri), so non-recognition means treating a son as an outsider.
'Hairy'. It recalls Esau's birth ('all over like a hairy mantle', 25:25) and the name Seir; the hairiness is the thing the whole disguise imitates.

verses.translation_literal: And he said, "[Are] you this, my son Esau?" And he said, "I [am]."
verses.translation_dramatic: Once more Isaac asked it, as if the answer might change: "Are you really my son Esau?" And from the dark in front of him, one small word: "I am."
verses.directors_commentary: Isaac asks a third time, so the narrator can show the lie told with care. The word for 'I' here is not the long anokhi of v. 19 but the short ani. Rashi notes that Jacob does not say 'I am Esau', only 'I am': the shortest possible answer, nearly true in a way. KJV 'I am' captures it. Radak says the repeated question is a kindness: Isaac does not want to insult Esau by doubting him, so he asks again and again.

philological_notes.note: 'I', the short form, where v. 19 used anokhi. Rashi stresses that Jacob did not say 'I am Esau'.

events.title: Isaac, old and blind, sends Esau to hunt
events.narrative_summary: Isaac, old and nearly blind, calls his elder son Esau. He says he does not know the day of his death and asks Esau to hunt game and prepare the food he loves, so that he may bless him before he dies.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: The text says only that Isaac was old and his eyes dim, with no number. I anchor on Isaac's birth with an offset of 123 years, Rashi's count at 27:2 (Seder Olam: Isaac 123, Jacob 63; Sarah died at 127 and Isaac was then 37). Margin 5 years because the age is the tradition's, not the text's. Tier MACRO_ERA. Pseudo-Jonathan's 14 Nisan is midrash and is not used. Duration 10 minutes for a short speech.
events.ancient_year_marker: When Isaac was old and his eyes were dim

events.title: Esau goes to the field to hunt
events.narrative_summary: While Rebekah listens, Esau goes out to the field to hunt game and bring it back.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Starts when Isaac finishes speaking (27:5, END of the commission, no delay). A hunt of about 3 hours is an estimate, with a margin of 30 minutes. No hour is given, so DAY_SEQUENCE for a continuous scene.

events.title: Rebekah tells Jacob to take Esau's blessing
events.narrative_summary: Rebekah repeats to Jacob what she heard and tells him to bring two kids so she can prepare the dish for Isaac and Jacob can receive the blessing. Jacob fears being found out and cursed. She takes the curse on herself.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: She heard the speech (27:5) and speaks once Esau has left. Offset 10 minutes after the end of the commission, so the conversation begins after Esau is gone; duration 15 minutes. No hour is given: DAY_SEQUENCE, the same continuous scene.

events.title: Jacob fetches the kids and Rebekah dresses him as Esau
events.narrative_summary: Jacob fetches two kids and brings them to his mother, who cooks the dish Isaac loves. She dresses Jacob in Esau's best garments, covers his hands and neck with the goatskins, and hands him the food and bread.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the conversation immediately (27:14, 'and he went'). About 2 hours to fetch and slaughter the kids, cook, and dress Jacob, estimated, margin 30 minutes. The text gives no hour.

events.title: Jacob passes himself off as Esau before Isaac
events.narrative_summary: Jacob brings the food and says he is Esau. Isaac doubts: the voice is Jacob's, the hands are Esau's, and the game came quickly. He feels Jacob's hands, asks again, and eats and drinks the wine.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Continues straight from the preparation (27:18). About 20 minutes for the questioning and the meal. Margin 15 minutes. No hour is named.

events.title: Isaac kisses and blesses Jacob
events.narrative_summary: Isaac asks Jacob to come close and kiss him, smells his garments, and blesses him with the dew of heaven, the fat of the earth and rule over his brothers.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Follows the meal at once (27:26, 'then Isaac said'). About 10 minutes for the kiss and the blessing, margin 10 minutes.

events.title: Esau returns and Isaac trembles at the deception
events.narrative_summary: Jacob has scarcely left when Esau comes in from hunting, makes his dish and brings it to Isaac. When Esau says who he is, Isaac trembles violently and says the blessing he gave cannot be taken back.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'Jacob had scarcely gone out' (27:30): Esau arrives minutes after the blessing ends. Offset 5 minutes from the END of the blessing, margin 1 hour. The event covers his arrival (27:30), his preparing the dish (27:31, 'he also made savoury meat', which takes about as long as Rebekah's cooking in kids_prepared) and the exchange with Isaac (27:31-33). Duration about 90 minutes (roughly 1 hour of cooking plus 30 minutes of speech), an estimate; the text gives no figure. Margin 1 hour on the same footing as kids_prepared.

events.title: Esau cries out and receives a lesser blessing
events.narrative_summary: Esau cries bitterly and asks for a blessing too. Isaac says Jacob took it by deceit. After Esau begs again, Isaac promises a dwelling away from the fat of the earth, life by the sword, service to his brother, and a time when he will break the yoke.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: Continues straight from Isaac's trembling (27:34), END anchor with no delay. About 20 minutes for the exchange, margin 10 minutes.

events.title: Esau hates Jacob and plans to kill him after Isaac's death
events.narrative_summary: Esau holds a grudge against Jacob because of the blessing and says in his heart that the days of mourning for his father are near, and then he will kill Jacob.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No delay is stated. I place it an hour after the lesser blessing, with a margin of 1 day, as a reaction to the scene. The stated intention is for after Isaac's death (Radak: not while Isaac lives). Tier DAY_SEQUENCE for a continuous scene, not a stated hour.

events.title: Rebekah tells Jacob to flee to Laban in Haran
events.narrative_summary: Esau's words are reported to Rebekah. She calls Jacob and tells him that Esau means to kill him. She orders him to flee to her brother Laban in Haran and stay a few days until Esau's anger passes, when she will send for him.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: 'It was told to Rebekah' (27:42) gives no interval; I take 1 day, margin 3 days. 'A few days' (27:44) is Rebekah's expectation: Ibn Ezra reads it as a few years (under ten), Radak as 'few'. The actual stay is not in this chapter.

events.title: Rebekah tells Isaac she loathes the Hittite women
events.narrative_summary: Rebekah tells Isaac she is weary of her life because of the daughters of Heth and asks what use her life would be if Jacob also took a Hittite wife.
events.temporal_reasoning_note: No date is given. I place it 1 day after the warning to Jacob, margin 5 days, following verse order. It leads to Isaac sending Jacob to Paddan-aram (28:1-5).

causal_edges.causal_explanation: Esau's words are reported to Rebekah, who sends Jacob away to save his life (27:42-43).
Esau's cry is the result of finding that Isaac has already blessed Jacob (27:33-34).
Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing his father gave him (27:41).
Isaac's request that Esau hunt and prepare food sends Esau into the field (27:3-5).
Rebekah overhears Isaac promising Esau a blessing and so devises a way for Jacob to receive it (27:5-10).
The dish and the disguise make it possible for Jacob to stand before Isaac as Esau (27:15-18).
Jacob obeys his mother's command and fetches the kids for the dish (27:13-14).
Rebekah gives Isaac the Hittite wives as her reason for sending Jacob to Haran, so as not to reveal Esau's threat (27:46); the link is inferred.

entities.etymology_meaning: The Hebrew describes them as 'desirable' or 'precious' (hachamudot).
entities.summary_bio: The fine garments Esau kept in Rebekah's house. She puts them on Jacob so that his smell will persuade the blind Isaac that he is Esau (27:15, 27).

entities.canonical_name: Kid Skins on Jacob's Hands and Neck
entities.etymology_meaning: The skins of the goat kids, put over Jacob's hands and the smooth of his neck.
entities.summary_bio: Rebekah covers Jacob's hands and neck with the skins of the two kids so that he will feel hairy like Esau (27:16). They defeat Isaac's touch test (27:22–23).

entities.etymology_meaning: Probably 'terror' or 'dread'; the name is of uncertain origin.
entities.summary_bio: Heth is the ancestor of the Hittites, a son of Canaan. In Genesis 27 Rebekah speaks of 'the daughters of Heth', the Hittite women among whom Esau has married, as the cause of her weariness with life.

entities.etymology_meaning: From ta'am, 'taste': dishes seasoned to the eater's liking.
entities.summary_bio: The favourite meal Isaac asks Esau to bring before blessing him (27:4). Rebekah makes it from two kids of the flock so that Jacob can bring it to Isaac in Esau's place.

components.evidence_explanation: 27:40: 'You shall serve your brother', in Isaac's words to Esau.
27:34: Esau cries out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry.

components.label_value: Hating Jacob and plotting to kill him
components.evidence_explanation: 27:41: Esau hated Jacob and said he would kill him after his father's mourning days.
27:15: Rebekah took Esau's best garments and put them on Jacob.
27:1: Isaac was old and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see.
27:15–16: Jacob wears Esau's clothes and the kid skins on his hands and neck; it lasts until 27:30, when Esau comes.
27:29: 'Be lord over your brothers'; 27:37: 'I have made him lord over you'.
27:27–29: Isaac blesses Jacob believing him to be Esau; 27:33 he confirms 'he shall be blessed'.

systems.name: Deceptive impersonation
systems.ancient_near_east_context: Passing oneself off as another, especially to a blind or distant superior, to obtain a legal benefit such as a blessing or inheritance. The narrators of Genesis treat it as deceit with consequences (27:35, 36).
rules_and_mechanics: The deceiver adopts the appearance, clothing, smell or voice of another.
The victim tests the claim by sense: voice, touch, taste, smell.
A false oath or invocation of God may reinforce the lie (27:20).
Successful deceit yields a benefit; discovery brings anger and flight.

systems.name: Patriarchal blessing
systems.ancient_near_east_context: In the patriarchal world a father's dying or near-dying blessing allocated the family's future: who leads, what land and fertility the sons receive. It was spoken aloud, often over a meal or with a kiss and touch, and was held to be effective by the word itself, often invoking God.
rules_and_mechanics: The father pronounces the blessing in the presence of the son, usually near death.
A meal and physical contact (kiss, touch, smell) accompany the rite.
The words bind the future; once spoken, it cannot be taken back (27:33, 37).
It may grant fertility of land, rule over brothers and the blessing of others who bless or curse the recipient.
It can be given in differentiated forms to different sons.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Isaac kisses Jacob, smells the garments and pronounces a blessing of dew, grain and wine, rule over nations and brothers, and blessings on those who bless him.
system_instances.significance_note: Transfers the firstborn blessing to Jacob and cannot be revoked, even when the mistake is discovered (27:33).

system_instances.outcome_summary: Rebekah cooks the kids as Isaac likes them and dresses Jacob in Esau's best clothes and the kid skins, then sends him in with the meal and bread.
system_instances.significance_note: Rebekah is the author of the plan; the preparations anticipate Isaac's senses of smell and touch.

system_instances.outcome_summary: Jacob tells Isaac 'I am Esau your firstborn', answers his questions with lies and invokes the LORD; Isaac feels the skins, hears Jacob's voice and finally believes the hands.
system_instances.significance_note: The deceit that gains the blessing and sets the family apart: Esau's later cry (27:35) names it.

system_instances.outcome_summary: After Esau's plea Isaac speaks a lesser word: a dwelling away from the fat of the earth, life by the sword, service to his brother, and a future breaking of the yoke.
system_instances.significance_note: Gives Esau a future but subordinate to Jacob, and prefigures the Edom–Israel relationship.

edges.description: Esau cries out bitterly and begs his father for a blessing too.
Esau hates Jacob and resolves to kill him after his father's death.
Isaac gives Esau a lesser blessing of a dwelling away from fertility, the sword and service to his brother.
Isaac blesses Jacob, taking him for Esau.
Isaac tells Esau to take his weapons, hunt game and prepare savory food so that Isaac can bless him.
Jacob tells his blind father 'I am Esau your firstborn' and brings him the meal.
Rebekah tells Isaac she is weary of life because of the Hittite women and that Jacob must not marry one.
Rebekah tells Jacob to obey her and fetch two kids so she can cook for Isaac.
Rebekah dresses Jacob in Esau's garments and covers his hands and neck with kid skins.
Rebekah tells Jacob to flee to her brother Laban in Haran until Esau's anger turns away.
